claim: Propagation of non-linear waves is key to the functioning of diverse biological systems.
source: Propagation of non-linear waves is key to the functioning of diverse biological systems.
evidence: This is a general statement about biological systems presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but draws on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Non-linear waves can organize into spirals, rotating around a core, whose properties determine the overall wave dynamics.
source: Such waves can organize into spirals, rotating around a core, whose properties determine the overall wave dynamics.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The theory that manipulation of a spiral wave core should lead to full spatiotemporal control over its dynamics lacks supportive evidence.
source: Theoretically, manipulation of a spiral wave core should lead to full spatiotemporal control over its dynamics. However, this theory lacks supportive evidence (even at a conceptual level), making it thus a long-standing hypothesis.
evidence: The authors state this as a gap in existing knowledge that their work addresses.

claim: The study proposes a new phenomenological concept that involves artificially dragging spiral waves by their cores.
source: Here, we propose a new phenomenological concept that involves artificially dragging spiral waves by their cores, to prove the aforementioned hypothesis in silico, with subsequent in vitro validation in optogenetically modified monolayers of rat atrial cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is the main claim of the study, supported by both computational and experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Core manipulation through controlled displacement of heterogeneities in excitable media allows forced movement of spiral waves along pre-defined trajectories.
source: We thereby connect previously established, but unrelated concepts of spiral wave attraction, anchoring and unpinning to demonstrate that core manipulation, through controlled displacement of heterogeneities in excitable media, allows forced movement of spiral waves along pre-defined trajectories.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental and computational results shown in Figures 1-5.

claim: The study imposes real-time spatiotemporal control over spiral wave dynamics in a biological system.
source: Consequently, we impose real-time spatiotemporal control over spiral wave dynamics in a biological system.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the in vitro experiments with optogenetically modified cardiomyocytes.

claim: Spiral waves are found in diverse natural systems including active galaxies.
source: Spiral waves are found in diverse natural systems: from active galaxies (Schulman and Seiden, 1986), to simple oscillatory chemical reactions (Belousov, 1985; Zhabotinsky, 1991), to social waves in colonies of giant honey bees (Kastberger et al., 2008), to Min protein gradients in bacterial cell division (Caspi and Dekker, 2016), and to the formation of vortices in fluids flowing past obstacles (Karman, 1937).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schulman and Seiden, 1986.

claim: Spiral waves are found in simple oscillatory chemical reactions.
source: Spiral waves are found in diverse natural systems: from active galaxies (Schulman and Seiden, 1986), to simple oscillatory chemical reactions (Belousov, 1985; Zhabotinsky, 1991), to social waves in colonies of giant honey bees (Kastberger et al., 2008), to Min protein gradients in bacterial cell division (Caspi and Dekker, 2016), and to the formation of vortices in fluids flowing past obstacles (Karman, 1937).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Belousov, 1985 and Zhabotinsky, 1991.

claim: Spiral waves are found in social waves in colonies of giant honey bees.
source: Spiral waves are found in diverse natural systems: from active galaxies (Schulman and Seiden, 1986), to simple oscillatory chemical reactions (Belousov, 1985; Zhabotinsky, 1991), to social waves in colonies of giant honey bees (Kastberger et al., 2008), to Min protein gradients in bacterial cell division (Caspi and Dekker, 2016), and to the formation of vortices in fluids flowing past obstacles (Karman, 1937).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kastberger et al., 2008.

claim: Spiral waves are found in Min protein gradients in bacterial cell division.
source: Spiral waves are found in diverse natural systems: from active galaxies (Schulman and Seiden, 1986), to simple oscillatory chemical reactions (Belousov, 1985; Zhabotinsky, 1991), to social waves in colonies of giant honey bees (Kastberger et al., 2008), to Min protein gradients in bacterial cell division (Caspi and Dekker, 2016), and to the formation of vortices in fluids flowing past obstacles (Karman, 1937).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Caspi and Dekker, 2016.

claim: Spiral waves are found in the formation of vortices in fluids flowing past obstacles.
source: Spiral waves are found in diverse natural systems: from active galaxies (Schulman and Seiden, 1986), to simple oscillatory chemical reactions (Belousov, 1985; Zhabotinsky, 1991), to social waves in colonies of giant honey bees (Kastberger et al., 2008), to Min protein gradients in bacterial cell division (Caspi and Dekker, 2016), and to the formation of vortices in fluids flowing past obstacles (Karman, 1937).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Karman, 1937.

claim: Spiral waves guide morphogenesis in slime molds.
source: While being beneficial to some systems, for example slime molds, where they guide morphogenesis, such activity has detrimental consequences for other systems including the heart, where they underlie lethal cardiac arrhythmias (Davidenko et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about slime molds.

claim: Spiral waves underlie lethal cardiac arrhythmias in the heart.
source: While being beneficial to some systems, for example slime molds, where they guide morphogenesis, such activity has detrimental consequences for other systems including the heart, where they underlie lethal cardiac arrhythmias (Davidenko et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Davidenko et al., 1990.

claim: Spiral wave activity organizes around an unexcitable center (core), whose properties determine its overall dynamics.
source: It has been reported that irrespective of the nature of the excitable medium, spiral wave activity organizes around an unexcitable center (core), whose properties determine its overall dynamics (Krinsky, 1978; Beaumont et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krinsky, 1978 and Beaumont et al., 1998.

claim: Spiral waves exhibit particle-like behavior attributed to an underlying topological charge.
source: Theorists attribute such particle-like behavior of a spiral wave to an underlying topological charge, which controls its short-range interaction, annihilation, and the ability to form intricate bound states with other spirals (Ermakova et al., 1989; Schebesch and Engel, 1999; Steinbock et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ermakova et al., 1989; Schebesch and Engel, 1999; Steinbock et al., 1992.

claim: Steinbock et al. (1993) demonstrated the possibility to forcibly anchor meandering spiral waves in an excitable light-sensitive Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction system.
source: To this end, a detailed mechanistic study was performed by Steinbock et al. (1993), who demonstrated the possibility to forcibly anchor meandering spiral waves in an excitable light-sensitive Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction system.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Steinbock et al., 1993.

claim: Ke et al. (2015) demonstrated that forced anchoring of scroll waves to thin glass rods, followed by subsequent movement of the rods themselves, could enable scroll wave relocation in a three-dimensional BZ reaction setting.
source: Furthermore, Ke et al. (2015) demonstrated in a three-dimensional BZ reaction setting, that forced anchoring of scroll waves to thin glass rods, followed by subsequent movement of the rods themselves, could enable scroll wave relocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ke et al., 2015.

claim: Functional and anatomical reentry are recognized as drivers of cardiac arrhythmias.
source: In cardiac tissue, the analogs of a classical spiral wave and a wave rotating around a heterogeneity, are, respectively, functional and anatomical reentry, both of which are recognized as drivers of arrhythmias.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in cardiac electrophysiology.

claim: Davidenko et al. (1991) demonstrated that a drifting spiral wave could anchor to an obstacle and thereby make a transition from functional to anatomical reentry.
source: Seminal findings by Davidenko et al. (1991) demonstrated that a drifting spiral wave could anchor to an obstacle and thereby make a transition from functional to anatomical reentry.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Davidenko et al., 1991.

claim: Ripplinger et al. (2006) showed that small electric shocks could unpin a reentrant wave rotating around an obstacle, bringing about the reverse transition from anatomical to functional reentry.
source: Conversely, Ripplinger et al. (2006) showed that small electric shocks could unpin a reentrant wave rotating around an obstacle, bringing about the reverse transition from anatomical to functional reentry.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ripplinger et al., 2006.

claim: Nakouzi et al. (2016) and Zykov et al. (2010) demonstrated that the transitions between anchored and free spiral states may be accompanied by hysteresis near the heterogeneities.
source: Nakouzi et al. (2016) and Zykov et al. (2010) demonstrated that the transitions between anchored and free spiral states may be accompanied by hysteresis near the heterogeneities.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nakouzi et al., 2016 and Zykov et al., 2010.

claim: Defauw et al. (2014) showed that small-sized anatomical heterogeneities could attract spiral waves from a close distance, and even lead to their termination if located near an unexcitable boundary.
source: Furthermore, Defauw et al. (2014) showed that small-sized anatomical heterogeneities could attract spiral waves from a close distance, and even lead to their termination if located near an unexcitable boundary.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Defauw et al., 2014.

claim: All studies dedicated to spiral wave attraction and anchoring involved the presence of anatomically predefined, permanent heterogeneities, or continuous-in-time processes.
source: However, to date, all studies dedicated to spiral wave attraction and anchoring involved the presence of anatomically predefined, permanent heterogeneities, or continuous-in-time processes, thereby making it impossible to manipulate spiral wave cores in a flexible, systematic and dynamical manner.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the limitations of previous studies, based on the authors' review of the literature.

claim: Optogenetics allows the creation of spatially and temporally predefined heterogeneities at superb resolution at any location within an excitable medium.
source: We establish such control through optogenetics (Boyden et al., 2005; Bi et al., 2006; Deisseroth, 2015; McNamara et al., 2016), which allows the creation of spatially and temporally predefined heterogeneities at superb resolution at any location within an excitable medium.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyden et al., 2005; Bi et al., 2006; Deisseroth, 2015; McNamara et al., 2016.

claim: Previous studies demonstrate the power of optogenetics in cardiac systems.
source: Previous studies for example by Arrenberg et al. (2010); Bruegmann et al. (2010); Jia et al. (2011); Bingen et al. (2014); Entcheva and Bub (2016) and Burton et al. (2015), demonstrate the power of optogenetics in cardiac systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arrenberg et al. (2010); Bruegmann et al. (2010); Jia et al. (2011); Bingen et al. (2014); Entcheva and Bub (2016) and Burton et al. (2015).

claim: Self-sustained spiral waves of period 60±5 ms were induced in silico in confluent monolayers of optogenetically modified neonatal rat atrial cardiomyocytes.
source: In this study, we induced spiral waves of period 60±5 ms in silico and of period 63±11 ms in vitro in confluent monolayers of optogenetically modified neonatal rat atrial cardiomyocytes (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from the study.

claim: Self-sustained spiral waves of period 63±11 ms were induced in vitro in confluent monolayers of optogenetically modified neonatal rat atrial cardiomyocytes.
source: In this study, we induced spiral waves of period 60±5 ms in silico and of period 63±11 ms in vitro in confluent monolayers of optogenetically modified neonatal rat atrial cardiomyocytes (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Targeted application of light to the monolayers led to the creation of a spatially predefined temporal heterogeneity (i.e. a reversible conduction block) near the core of a spiral wave.
source: Targeted application of light to the monolayers led to the sequential occurrence of two events: (i) creation of a spatially predefined temporal heterogeneity (i.e. a reversible conduction block) near the core of a spiral wave, and (ii) emergence of a wave from the spot of illumination.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental observations described in the Results section.

claim: Targeted application of light to the monolayers led to the emergence of a wave from the spot of illumination.
source: Targeted application of light to the monolayers led to the sequential occurrence of two events: (i) creation of a spatially predefined temporal heterogeneity (i.e. a reversible conduction block) near the core of a spiral wave, and (ii) emergence of a wave from the spot of illumination.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental observations described in the Results section.

claim: Feola et al. (2017) demonstrated the possibility to create a temporal heterogeneity with optical control over the size, location and duration of the block.
source: In a previous study (Feola et al., 2017), we demonstrated the possibility to create such a temporal heterogeneity with optical control over the size, location and duration of the block.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Feola et al., 2017.

claim: Creation of a light-induced block close to the core of a spiral wave can attract the spiral wave tip, causing it to eventually anchor to the block.
source: Here, we show how creation of a light-induced block close to the core of a spiral wave, can attract the spiral wave tip, causing it to eventually anchor to the block.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental and computational data presented in the Results section.

claim: Subsequent movement of the light spot to different locations within the monolayer results in dragging of the spiral wave along a predefined pathway of illumination.
source: Subsequent movement of the light spot to different locations within the monolayer, results in dragging of the spiral wave along a predefined pathway of illumination, thereby giving rise to, what we call Attract-Anchor-Drag-based (AAD) control.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental and computational data presented in Figures 1-5.

claim: It is possible to directly and precisely manipulate the spatial location of a stable spiral wave core.
source: Thus, we prove that it is indeed possible to directly and precisely manipulate the spatial location of a stable spiral wave core, and thereby overcome the constraints imposed by internal and external factors that shape the natural meander and drift trajectories.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental and computational results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Figure-of-eight type reentry can be removed efficiently by dragging the cores of both spiral waves towards each other, till their phase singularities collide, leading to self-annihilation.
source: In silico, we find that figure-of-eight type reentry can be removed efficiently by dragging the cores of both spiral waves towards each other, till their phase singularities collide, leading to self-annihilation.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data shown in Figure 4.

claim: At small d, the spiral tip is dragged along a cycloidal path, in which, the diameter of the loop is O(d).
source: At small d, the spiral tip is dragged along a cycloidal path, in which, the diameter of the loop is O(d).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: As d increases, the spiral tends to translate linearly, without executing rotational movement about the core.
source: As d increases, the spiral tends to translate linearly, without executing rotational movement about the core.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Probability of attraction depends on the phase of the spiral wave rotation at the moment of light exposure.
source: We find that probability of attraction also depends on the phase of the spiral wave rotation at the moment of light exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: A spiral wave cannot be dragged when r > 5.63 mm.
source: A spiral wave cannot be dragged when r > 5.63 mm.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Successful AAD control necessitates the spiral wave to make alternate transitions between functional (free) and anatomical (anchored) types of reentry.
source: Our in silico findings indicate that successful control necessitates the spiral wave to make alternate transitions between functional (free) and anatomical (anchored) types of reentry.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: When a spot of light is applied reasonably close to the core of a spiral wave, within the allowed Δθ, it creates a region of light-induced depolarization that attracts and anchors the core of the free spiral, thereby effectuating a transition from functional to anatomical reentry.
source: When a spot of light is applied reasonably close to the core of a spiral wave, within the allowed Δθ, it creates a region of light-induced depolarization that attracts and anchors the core of the free spiral, thereby effectuating a transition from functional to anatomical reentry.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis and represents a mechanistic explanation of the observed phenomenon.

claim: When the light spot is moved to a different location, still within the basin of attraction of the first light spot, the previously depolarized region recovers, forcing the anchored spiral to unpin and make a reverse transition to functional reentry.
source: When the light spot is now moved to a different location, still within the basin of attraction of the first light spot, the previously depolarized region recovers, forcing the anchored spiral to unpin and make a reverse transition to functional reentry.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis and represents a mechanistic explanation of the observed phenomenon.

claim: The study is one of the first to demonstrate the establishment of real-time spatiotemporal control over spiral wave dynamics in spatially extended biological (cardiac) tissue.
source: Our study is one of the first to demonstrate the establishment of real-time spatiotemporal control over spiral wave dynamics in spatially extended biological (cardiac) tissue.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work, based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Burton et al. (2015) use dynamic control to modulate spiral wave chirality, which is markedly different from spiral wave dragging.
source: The only other study that shows effective dynamic spatiotemporal control (as opposed to elimination) of spiral waves is that of (Burton et al., 2015). However, Burton et al. (2015) use dynamic control to modulate spiral wave chirality, which is markedly different from what we study and prove, namely spiral wave dragging.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Burton et al., 2015 and comparison with the current work.

claim: Previous researchers employed different kinds of spatiotemporal feedback interactions to control spiral wave dynamics in non-biological media.
source: In the past, researchers also employed different kinds of spatiotemporal feedback interactions to control spiral wave dynamics, albeit in non-biological media (Sakurai et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sakurai et al., 2002.

claim: Phase-based pulse delivery methods can be quite challenging in complex biological tissue, where temporal precision is a major subtlety and therefore difficult to achieve.
source: Although feasible in simple chemical systems, phase-based pulse delivery can be quite challenging in complex biological tissue, where temporal precision is a major subtlety and therefore difficult to achieve.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' understanding of the challenges in biological systems.

claim: Ke et al. (2015) demonstrate a process that is continuous in time, as opposed to the discrete nature of the AAD method.
source: The study by Ke et al. (2015) bypasses this issue by forcing scroll wave filaments to anchor to physical heterogeneities, which can be moved subsequently to steer the waves. However, Ke et al. (2015) demonstrate a process that is continuous in time, as opposed to the discrete nature of our method, which makes it more flexible.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with the cited work and the current study.

claim: The mechanism of attraction of spiral waves to localized heterogeneities is a generic phenomenon, observed among spiral waves in heterogeneous tissue.
source: Previous studies have explored the concept of spiral attraction in human cardiac tissue (Defauw et al., 2014). According to these findings, the mechanism of attraction of spiral waves to localized heterogeneities is a generic phenomenon, observed among spiral waves in heterogeneous tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Defauw et al., 2014.

claim: Spiral waves tend to drift to regions with longer rotational periods, that is where the duration of an action potential is longer than elsewhere in the medium.
source: Some studies (Defauw et al., 2014; Panfilov and Vasiev, 1991; Rudenko and Panfilov, 1983) show that spiral waves tend to drift to regions with longer rotational periods, that is where the duration of an action potential is longer than elsewhere in the medium.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Defauw et al., 2014; Panfilov and Vasiev, 1991; Rudenko and Panfilov, 1983.

claim: Application of a spot of light to a monolayer of excitable, optogenetically modified cardiomyocytes causes the cells in this region to depolarize, bearing a direct influence on the action potential duration of cells in the immediate neighborhood.
source: This is in consonance with our simulations, where application of a spot of light to a monolayer of excitable, optogenetically modified cardiomyocytes causes the cells in this region to depolarize, bearing a direct influence on the action potential duration of cells in the immediate neighborhood.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational simulations described in the study.

claim: AAD control is associated with repeated alternative transitions between functional and anatomical reentry.
source: Thus, AAD control is associated with repeated alternative transitions between functional and anatomical reentry.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on the computational and experimental observations.

claim: When an existing vortex interacts with a circular wave emerging from a stimulus applied close to the vortex core, they fail to annihilate each other according to Krinsky et al. (1995).
source: A mechanism, somewhat along the same lines as AAD control, was demonstrated by Krinsky et al. (1995), using topological considerations. When an existing vortex interacts with a circular wave emerging from a stimulus applied close to the vortex core, they fail to annihilate each other.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Krinsky et al., 1995.

claim: The emergent wave quenches the vortex, resulting in its displacement by the order of half a wavelength according to Krinsky et al. (1995).
source: However, the emergent wave quenches the vortex, resulting in its displacement by the order of half a wavelength.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Krinsky et al., 1995.

claim: Guo et al. (2010) investigated control of spiral wave turbulence in a self-regulation system that spontaneously eliminated vortex cores, by trapping the latter with localized inhomogeneities.
source: In another study (Guo et al., 2010), control of spiral wave turbulence was investigated in a self-regulation system that spontaneously eliminated vortex cores, by trapping the latter with localized inhomogeneities.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2010.

claim: Movement of a spiral wave along a line of predefined obstacles was observed by Andreev (2005).
source: Movement of a spiral wave along a line of predefined obstacles was also observed by Andreev (2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Andreev, 2005.

claim: Zykov et al. (2010) and Nakouzi et al. (2016) reported the involvement of bistability and hysteresis in the transitions from anchoring to unpinning of a wave rotating around an anatomical hole.
source: Based on their experimental, computational and theoretical studies, Zykov et al. (2010) and Nakouzi et al. (2016) reported the involvement of bistability and hysteresis in the transitions from anchoring to unpinning of a wave rotating around an anatomical hole.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zykov et al., 2010 and Nakouzi et al., 2016.

claim: Cardiac tissue possesses an inherently irregular discrete cellular structure, underlying the absence of spatial symmetries.
source: Compared to other systems, such as the BZ reaction, cardiac tissue (i) possesses an inherently irregular discrete cellular structure, underlying the absence of spatial symmetries, (ii) lacks inhibitor diffusion and (iii) has different dimensions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cardiac tissue structure.

claim: Cardiac tissue lacks inhibitor diffusion.
source: Compared to other systems, such as the BZ reaction, cardiac tissue (i) possesses an inherently irregular discrete cellular structure, underlying the absence of spatial symmetries, (ii) lacks inhibitor diffusion and (iii) has different dimensions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cardiac tissue properties.

claim: Previous studies demonstrated alternative methods to 'control' spiral-wave dynamics in excitable media by periodic forcing to induce resonant drift.
source: Previous studies also demonstrated alternative methods to 'control' spiral-wave dynamics in excitable media, for example, by periodic forcing to induce resonant drift (Agladze et al., 1987; Biktasheva et al., 1999; Agladze et al., 2007), or by periodic modulation of excitability to manipulate spiral tip trajectories (Steinbock et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Agladze et al., 1987; Biktasheva et al., 1999; Agladze et al., 2007.

claim: Previous studies demonstrated alternative methods to 'control' spiral-wave dynamics in excitable media by periodic modulation of excitability to manipulate spiral tip trajectories.
source: Previous studies also demonstrated alternative methods to 'control' spiral-wave dynamics in excitable media, for example, by periodic forcing to induce resonant drift (Agladze et al., 1987; Biktasheva et al., 1999; Agladze et al., 2007), or by periodic modulation of excitability to manipulate spiral tip trajectories (Steinbock et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Steinbock et al., 1993.

claim: The principal limitation of previous control methods is that they are indirect, giving reasonable control over the initial and final states of the system, with little or no control in between.
source: However, the principal limitation of these methods is that they are indirect, giving reasonable control over the initial and final states of the system, with little or no control in between.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' analysis of previous methods.

claim: AAD control allows precise and complete spatiotemporal control over spiral wave dynamics in two-dimensional excitable media.
source: It is herein where lies the advantage of AAD control, which allows precise and complete spatiotemporal control over spiral wave dynamics in two-dimensional excitable media.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental and computational results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The penetration depth of light in cardiac tissue is relatively short.
source: Since the penetration depth of light in cardiac tissue is relatively short (Bruegmann et al., 2016), full transmural illumination might be challenging, particularly in ventricles of large mammals like pig, monkey or human.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bruegmann et al., 2016.

claim: Full transmural illumination might be challenging in ventricles of large mammals like pig, monkey or human.
source: Since the penetration depth of light in cardiac tissue is relatively short (Bruegmann et al., 2016), full transmural illumination might be challenging, particularly in ventricles of large mammals like pig, monkey or human.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limited penetration depth of light in cardiac tissue.

claim: AAD control may provide a powerful tool to regulate scroll wave dynamics by epicardial or endocardial illumination.
source: There, AAD control may provide a powerful tool to regulate scroll wave dynamics by epicardial or endocardial illumination.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future applications.

claim: The electrophysiological properties of neonatal rat atrial cardiomyocytes were modeled according to Majumder et al. (2016).
source: The electrophysiological properties of neonatal rat atrial cardiomyocytes were modeled according to Majumder et al. (2016), whereby, the transmembrane potential V of a single cell evolved in time as follows:
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Majumder et al., 2016.

claim: The signal conduction velocity in the simulations was 22.2±3.4 cm/s.
source: This resulted in a signal conduction velocity of 22.2±3.4 cm/s.
evidence: This is a result from the computational simulations.

claim: The optogenetic tool used in the numerical studies was a model of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii channelrhodopsin-2 mutant H134R, adopted from the studies of Boyle et al. (2013).
source: The optogenetic tool used in the numerical studies was a model of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii channelrhodopsin-2 mutant H134R, adopted from the studies of Boyle et al. (2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Boyle et al., 2013.

claim: The simulation domains were composed of neonatal rat atrial cardiomyocytes with 17% randomly distributed cardiac fibroblasts.
source: In order to be consistent with the in vitro experiments, we prepared 10 different simulation domains, composed of neonatal rat atrial cardiomyocytes with 17% randomly distributed cardiac fibroblasts (MacCannell et al., 2007) and with natural cellular heterogeneity, modelled as per (Majumder et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the composition of the computational model, supported by citations.

claim: All animal experiments were reviewed and approved by the Animal Experiments Committee of the Leiden University Medical Center.
source: All animal experiments were reviewed and approved by the Animal Experiments Committee of the Leiden University Medical Center and conformed to the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals as stated by the US National Institutes of Health.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the experiments.

claim: The neonatal rat atrial cardiomyocyte monolayers were incubated for 20-24 hr with CatCh-encoding lentiviral particles at a dose resulting in homogeneous transduction of nearly 100% of the cells.
source: At day 4 of culture, the neonatal rat atrial cardiomyocyte monolayers were incubated for 20 – 24 hr with CatCh-encoding lentiviral particles at a dose resulting in homogeneous transduction of nearly 100% of the cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used to create the optogenetically modified cells.

claim: Optical voltage mapping was used to investigate optogenetic manipulation of spiral wave dynamics in the CatCh-expressing monolayers on day 7 of culture.
source: Optical voltage mapping was used to investigate optogenetic manipulation of spiral wave dynamics in the CatCh-expressing monolayers on day 7 of culture by using the voltage-sensitive dye di-4-ANBDQBS (52.5 μM final concentration; ITK diagnostics, Uithoorn, the Netherlands), as described previously (Feola et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, supported by citation.

claim: CatCh was locally activated by using a patterned illumination device (Polygon400; Mightex Systems, Toronto, ON) connected to a 470-nm, high-power collimator light-emitting diode (LED) source.
source: CatCh was locally activated by using a patterned illumination device (Polygon400; Mightex Systems, Toronto, ON) connected to a 470-nm, high-power collimator light-emitting diode (LED) source (type-H, also from Mightex Systems).
evidence: This describes the experimental equipment used for optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Reentry was induced by light-based stimulations in 18 monolayers.
source: Before local optogenetic manipulation, reentry was induced by light-based stimulations (n = 18).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol and sample size.

claim: The spiral wave core can be dragged along a predefined 9-step triangular path in silico and in vitro.
source: Figure 1 (C1-4) and 1(D1-4) show representative examples of AAD control of spiral wave dynamics in silico and in vitro, respectively, where the spiral wave core is dragged along a predefined 9-step triangular path (see also Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: A single spiral wave can be removed in silico with a five-step drag sequence of circular light spots of 0.275 cm diameter and 250 ms illumination time per spot.
source: We first focus on removing a single spiral wave in silico (Figures 2 A1–5; see also Video 2). With a five-step drag sequence of circular light spots of 0.275 cm diameter and 250 ms illumination time per spot, we demonstrate the possibility to remove a spiral wave from a monolayer, by capturing its core somewhere near the middle of the simulation domain and subsequently dragging it all the way to the unexcitable boundary on the left, causing the phase singularity to collide with the border and annihilate.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data shown in Figure 2A and Video 2.

claim: In vitro findings corroborate the in silico results for single spiral wave termination.
source: Inspired by the outcome of our in silico experiments, we tested the same principle in vitro, with a five-step drag sequence of circular light spots with similar characteristics as those applied in silico. Our in vitro findings corroborate the in silico results (Figures 2 B1–5; see also Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Video 2.

claim: Figure-of-eight type reentry can be terminated in vitro by dragging the cores of both spiral waves toward each other to make them collide and annihilate.
source: Figure 4 (B1-6) (see also Video 3) show successful experimental (in vitro) validation of our in silico findings, following the same termination protocol.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Video 3.

claim: Complex reentry pattern characterized by four phase singularities can be terminated in vitro using AAD control.
source: A similar strategy applied in vitro enabled successful termination of a complex reentry pattern characterized by four phase singularities. This is illustrated in Figure 5 (C1-7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.
